azure-4.title: Azure Functions with Dynamics 365: Webhooks vs Service Bus for Dataverse Events (Part 4)
azure-4.html:
📚 This is Part 4 of my series "Azure Functions with Dynamics 365". New here? Start with Part 1, or read the previous one: Part 3: Heavy Dataverse workloads with Durable Functions.

Why this part comes next

In Part 3, Durable Functions processed 250,000 Dataverse records without timing out. But every one of those designs starts with the same question: how does Azure even know that something changed in Dynamics 365?

This part answers that. Dataverse can push an event to Azure the moment a record is saved, in two ways: a webhook or a Service Bus endpoint. Choosing the wrong one is behind many "the integration worked in testing" stories.

The scenario: an instant credit check

A bank manages loan applications in Dynamics 365, in a custom table called Loan Application (new_loanapplication). About 400 applications are created on a normal day, and up to 8,000 when the marketing team runs a bulk import from a campaign.

The business wants a credit score on every new application within seconds, without anyone clicking a button.

Why polling fails

The first idea is usually a scheduled job that asks Dataverse "any new applications?" every 15 minutes.

  • It is late. A loan officer can wait up to 15 minutes for a score.
  • It wastes calls. 96 runs a day, and most of them find nothing.
  • It struggles with spikes. On bulk import days, one run suddenly picks up thousands of records at once.

Polling: a job asks for new records every 15 minutes. Up to 15 minutes late, many wasted calls. Push (webhook or Service Bus): Dataverse sends the event the moment the record is saved. Seconds, no wasted calls.

The fix is to let Dataverse push the event to us. A real-life comparison: you don't phone the restaurant every 2 minutes to ask if your biryani is ready. The delivery app notifies you when the order is picked up. That notification is a push.

Two ways Dataverse pushes an event

Both options are built into Dataverse and registered with the same tool (the Plugin Registration Tool). Both send the same data: the RemoteExecutionContext, the same context a plugin receives.

  • Webhook. Dataverse calls an HTTP URL you own, usually an Azure Function with an HTTP trigger. Simple and direct.
  • Service Bus endpoint. Dataverse posts the context as a message to an Azure Service Bus queue or topic. Your Azure Function reads from the queue at its own pace.

A webhook is like a phone call: the other side must pick up now. A Service Bus endpoint is like a letterbox: the letter waits until someone collects it.

What happens when a loan application is saved

  1. A loan officer saves a new Loan Application.
  2. Dataverse finds a registered step for Create on new_loanapplication.
  3. For an asynchronous step, Dataverse creates a background system job. The user's save finishes immediately.
  4. The job sends the context out: as an HTTP POST to the webhook URL, or as a message on the Service Bus queue.
  5. The Azure Function runs. It calls the credit bureau and writes the score back through the Dataverse Web API.
  6. The officer refreshes the form and sees the score.

In synchronous mode, step 3 is skipped. Dataverse calls the endpoint straight away and the user's save waits for the reply. Any response other than 2xx counts as a failure.

Why an Azure Function and not a plugin?

Plugins run inside the Dataverse sandbox, with a 2-minute limit and restricted network access. The credit bureau call needs secrets from Key Vault, external libraries and retry logic. All of that is easier and safer in an Azure Function.

Hands-on 1: a webhook calling an Azure Function

What you need: an Azure subscription, a Dynamics 365 / Dataverse environment where you are System Administrator, Visual Studio or VS Code with the Azure Functions tools, and the Plugin Registration Tool (open it with "pac tool prt" from the Power Platform CLI).

Step 1: Create the Azure Function

Create an Azure Functions project (.NET isolated worker) with an HTTP trigger and authorization level Function. Replace the function with this code: 

using System.Text.Json;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

public class LoanCreditCheck
{
    private readonly ILogger<LoanCreditCheck> _logger;
    public LoanCreditCheck(ILogger<LoanCreditCheck> logger) => _logger = logger;

    [Function("LoanCreditCheck")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post")] HttpRequest req)
    {
        // 1. Read the payload Dataverse sent
        string body = await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync();
        using JsonDocument doc = JsonDocument.Parse(body);
        JsonElement ctx = doc.RootElement;

        // 2. Basic facts about the event
        string message  = ctx.GetProperty("MessageName").GetString();       // e.g. Create
        string table    = ctx.GetProperty("PrimaryEntityName").GetString(); // e.g. new_loanapplication
        string recordId = ctx.GetProperty("PrimaryEntityId").GetString();
        _logger.LogInformation("{Message} on {Table} {Id}", message, table, recordId);

        // 3. TODO: call the credit bureau API and update the record
        //    using the Dataverse Web API (ServiceClient + app registration)

        // 4. Return 200 so Dataverse knows it worked
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

Publish it to Azure. In the portal, open the function, choose Get function URL, and copy two things: the URL without the ?code= part, and the function key.

Step 2: Register the webhook

  1. Open the Plugin Registration Tool and connect to your environment.
  2. Choose Register → Register New Web Hook.
  3. Name = LoanCreditCheckHook. Endpoint URL = the function URL without ?code=.
  4. Authentication = WebhookKey, Value = the function key. Dataverse adds it as ?code=<key> on every call.
  5. Save.

Step 3: Register a step (when should it fire?)

The webhook alone does nothing. A step tells Dataverse which event triggers it.

  1. Right-click the webhook → Register New Step.
  2. Message = Create, Primary Entity = new_loanapplication.
  3. Event Pipeline Stage = PostOperation (the record is already saved).
  4. Execution Mode = Asynchronous (the user does not wait).
  5. Register the step.

Step 4: Test it

  1. Create a new Loan Application in Dynamics 365.
  2. In Azure, open the function's Log stream or Application Insights. You should see "Create on new_loanapplication <id>".
  3. If nothing arrives, go to Settings → System Jobs in Dynamics 365 and look for a failed job with the error message.

Hands-on 2: the same event through Service Bus

Now the bulk-import day. 8,000 applications arrive in an hour, and the credit bureau allows only a few calls per second. A webhook would hit the Function 8,000 times as fast as Dataverse can send them. With Service Bus, the messages wait in a queue and the Function works through them at a safe pace.

Step 1: Create the queue

  1. In the Azure portal, create a Service Bus namespace (Standard tier) and a queue called loan-events.
  2. Under the namespace, open Shared access policies and create a policy with Send rights for Dataverse. Copy its connection string.
  3. Create a second policy with Listen rights for the Azure Function.

Step 2: Register the Service Bus endpoint

  1. In the Plugin Registration Tool, choose Register → Register New Service Endpoint.
  2. Paste the Send connection string.
  3. Designation Type = Queue, Queue name = loan-events.
  4. Message Format = JSON, so the Function can read it easily.
  5. Save, then register a step on the endpoint exactly as before: Create, new_loanapplication, PostOperation, Asynchronous.

Step 3: The Service Bus-triggered Function 

using System.Text.Json;
using Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus;
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

public class LoanEventProcessor
{
    private readonly ILogger<LoanEventProcessor> _logger;
    public LoanEventProcessor(ILogger<LoanEventProcessor> logger) => _logger = logger;

    [Function("LoanEventProcessor")]
    public async Task Run(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("loan-events", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")]
        ServiceBusReceivedMessage message)
    {
        // 1. The body is the RemoteExecutionContext in JSON
        using JsonDocument doc = JsonDocument.Parse(message.Body.ToString());
        string recordId = doc.RootElement.GetProperty("PrimaryEntityId").GetString();
        _logger.LogInformation("Message {MessageId} for loan {RecordId}", message.MessageId, recordId);

        // 2. TODO: skip if this loan already has a score (safe to run twice)
        // 3. TODO: call the credit bureau and write the score back via the Web API

        // If this method throws, Service Bus delivers the message again.
        // After the queue's max delivery count, it moves to the dead-letter queue.
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Put the Listen connection string in the app setting ServiceBusConnection, or better, use a managed identity with the Azure Service Bus Data Receiver role so there is no secret at all.

To protect the credit bureau, limit how many messages the Function handles at once with maxConcurrentCalls under the Service Bus settings in host.json.

How to decide: four questions

The registration is the easy part. Before I register anything, I ask four questions.

  1. Must the user wait? If the result must block a bad save, use synchronous. Everything else (scoring, notifications, syncing) should be asynchronous. A slow credit bureau should never block a loan officer.
  2. What if the receiver is down? A webhook has no queue in between. A Service Bus endpoint keeps the message safe until the Function is back.
  3. How much volume? A few events an hour: a webhook is simple and enough. Thousands in a burst, or a slow downstream API: Service Bus, so the Function works at its own pace.
  4. What if it arrives twice? Both options deliver "at least once". Retries can send the same event again, so the Function must be safe to run twice (idempotent).

Synchronous vs asynchronous

  • User waits? Synchronous: yes, the save waits for your endpoint. Asynchronous: no, it runs in the background.
  • If the call fails: Synchronous: the save fails and is rolled back; the user sees an error. Asynchronous: a failed system job is logged; the record stays saved.
  • Retries: Synchronous: none; the user must try again. Asynchronous: Dataverse retries the system job.
  • Use it for: Synchronous: validation that must block a bad save. Asynchronous: scoring, notifications, syncing to other systems.

Webhook authentication options

When you register a webhook, you choose how Dataverse proves it is allowed to call your URL:

  • WebhookKey adds ?code=<key> to the URL. Made for Azure Functions keys.
  • HttpHeader adds headers you define, such as an API key header.
  • HttpQueryString adds query string parameters you define.

Never leave the Function at authorization level Anonymous in production.

What the payload contains

The JSON is the RemoteExecutionContext. The properties you will use most:

  • MessageName: Create, Update, Delete and so on
  • PrimaryEntityName and PrimaryEntityId: which table and which record
  • InputParameters: key/value pairs; the Target entry holds the record's columns
  • PreEntityImages and PostEntityImages: the record before and after, if you registered images
  • UserId and InitiatingUserId: who triggered it

Very large webhook payloads are trimmed, and a header tells you data was removed. Treat the event as a signal: when in doubt, read the full record from the Web API using PrimaryEntityId.

Common mistakes

  1. Pasting the full URL with ?code= into Endpoint URL. Put the bare URL there and the key in the WebhookKey value, or the key is duplicated or exposed.
  2. Registering the endpoint but forgetting the step. Without a step, nothing ever fires.
  3. Synchronous mode for slow work. The user waits, and any timeout or error blocks their save.
  4. Long work before replying to a webhook. Return 200 quickly. For heavy work, put a message on a Service Bus queue and process it in a second Function.
  5. Firing on every Update. Set Filtering Attributes on the step so it fires only when the columns you care about change.
  6. An infinite loop. The Function updates the same record, which fires the event again. Filter on columns the Function never writes, or skip calls made by the integration user.
  7. Not handling duplicates. Make the logic safe to run twice, for example by checking whether a score already exists.
  8. No logging. Turn on Application Insights from day one, and watch the dead-letter queue as closely as production errors.

Webhook, Service Bus, plugin or Power Automate?

  • Plugin runs inside the Dataverse sandbox. Best for fast validation and logic close to the data. Watch out for the 2-minute limit and restricted network access.
  • Webhook calls your own HTTP endpoint, e.g. an Azure Function. Best for real-time calls to code you control. Watch out: your endpoint must be up, and there is no queue in between.
  • Service Bus endpoint posts to an Azure Service Bus queue or topic. Best for high volume, slow receivers and decoupled processing. Watch out: more setup, and it needs a consumer.
  • Power Automate runs cloud flows. Best for low-code automation by makers. Watch out: it runs after the save, with licensing and throttling limits.

Rule of thumb: a direct, simple call to your own code, use a webhook. The receiver might be down or the volume is high, use Service Bus.

Interview questions

  1. What is a Dataverse webhook, and how is it different from a plugin? A webhook sends the execution context to an external URL. A plugin runs your .NET code inside Dataverse.
  2. When would you choose a Service Bus endpoint over a webhook? When the receiver may be down, volume comes in bursts, or the downstream API must be protected. The queue holds messages until they are processed.
  3. What happens if a synchronous webhook fails? The operation fails, the transaction is rolled back and the user sees an error.
  4. Which authentication types can a webhook use? WebhookKey, HttpHeader and HttpQueryString.
  5. How do you avoid an infinite loop when the Function updates the same record? Use filtering attributes, avoid writing those columns, or skip calls made by the integration user.
  6. Why must the consumer be idempotent? Both options deliver at least once, so retries can bring the same event twice.

Conclusion

Webhooks and Service Bus endpoints let Dynamics 365 tell Azure about changes the moment they happen, with no polling. Register the endpoint, add a step, choose async for anything slow, secure it, and make the Function safe to run twice.

The choice comes down to one question: can the receiver keep up right now? If yes, a webhook is enough. If not, put Service Bus in between.

Next in the series: Part 5, what happens after the message arrives: retries, dead-letter queues and duplicate handling.

azure-1.title: Azure Functions with Dynamics 365 CRM (Dataverse): Beginner Tutorial
azure-1.html:
📚 This is Part 1 of my series "Azure Functions with Dynamics 365". In this beginner guide, I walk through real use cases for each way to trigger an Azure Function from Dynamics 365 (webhooks, Service Bus queues and Logic Apps), with C# code for each.

Azure Functions with Dynamics 365 CRM (Dataverse): Beginner Tutorial

Azure Functions is a serverless, event-driven compute service that runs your custom code in the cloud when triggered by events. You focus on writing the code you need, and Azure handles servers, scaling, and infrastructure. For example, imagine Azure Functions as a programmable sensor or smart switch: it stays idle until an event (like an HTTP call or a message) “flips the switch,” then your C# code runs on demand. Azure Functions supports many built-in triggers (HTTP, timers, queues, etc.) to connect with other services.

In a Dynamics CRM context, you could use Azure Functions whenever a CRM event needs extra processing. For instance, when a new Contact is created in CRM, a webhook or workflow step could call an Azure Function that sends a welcome email. Or when a record is updated, an Azure Function might log changes or call an external API. In each case, Azure Functions lets you write just the business logic in C# without managing a server or plugin, scaling up only when these events happen.

2. Using Webhooks

Dynamics 365 supports webhooks – a simple HTTP callback mechanism – to connect CRM events with external services. Starting in Dynamics 365 v9, you can configure a webhook so that when a CRM event occurs, CRM makes an HTTP POST (with JSON data) to the external URL. In practice, you register your Azure Function’s URL as a service endpoint in the Plugin Registration tool, and attach it to an entity event (e.g. Create of Contact). CRM will then invoke your function when that event happens. The webhook POST contains the record data in JSON, which your function can parse (as noted, “Webhooks send POST requests with JSON payload and can be consumed by any programming language”).

When a new Contact is created (Send Welcome Email)

Concept: Register a webhook on the Contact Create event. CRM will POST the new contact’s data to your Azure Function’s HTTP trigger. In the function, read the contact’s name and email and send a welcome message (e.g. via SendGrid or other email API). For simplicity below, the code just logs the email action. 

using System.IO;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http;
using Microsoft.Azure.WebJobs;
using Microsoft.Azure.WebJobs.Extensions.Http;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using Newtonsoft.Json;

public static class ContactCreatedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("ContactCreatedFunction")]
    public static async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Webhook received: new Contact created.");
        string json = await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync();
        dynamic data = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json);
        string name = data?.fullname;
        string email = data?.emailaddress1;
        // (In a real function, call an email service here)
        log.LogInformation($"Welcome email sent to {email} (Contact: {name}).");
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

When an Account is updated (Log changes)

Concept: Set up a webhook on the Account Update event. When an account changes, CRM sends the updated data to your function. The function reads key fields and logs them or forwards them to an external system. In the example below, we parse the account ID and name from the JSON payload and log it. 

public static class AccountUpdatedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("AccountUpdatedFunction")]
    public static IActionResult Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Webhook received: Account updated.");
        string json = new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEnd();
        dynamic data = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json);
        string accountId = data?.accountid;
        string accountName = data?.name;
        log.LogInformation($"Account updated: ID={accountId}, Name={accountName}");
        // (Additional code could post changes to an external API or database)
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

When a Lead is qualified (Notify Sales Manager)

Concept: Use a webhook on the Lead Qualify message (or a field that indicates qualification). When a lead is qualified, CRM sends lead details to your function. The function might then notify the sales manager (e.g. by email or Microsoft Teams). In this code, we extract the lead’s name and a manager email from the JSON and log a notification. 

public static class LeadQualifiedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("LeadQualifiedFunction")]
    public static async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Webhook received: Lead qualified.");
        string json = await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync();
        dynamic data = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json);
        string leadName = data?.leadid?.Name;
        string managerEmail = data?.manageremail; // assume field with manager email
        // (In a real function, send an email or Teams message to the manager)
        log.LogInformation($"Sales manager notified ({managerEmail}) that lead \"{leadName}\" was qualified.");
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

3. Using Service Bus Queues

For scenarios where you want reliable queuing or batch processing, Dynamics CRM can send messages to an Azure Service Bus queue instead of calling a webhook. You would typically use a custom plugin or workflow action in CRM that sends a Service Bus message. Then your Azure Function uses the ServiceBus trigger to process each message. As Microsoft notes, “Both webhooks and Azure Service Bus can be invoked from a plugin or custom workflow activity”. A ServiceBus-triggered function listens to a queue (or topic) and runs whenever a message arrives.

When a Case is closed (Send to Ticketing System)

Concept: Register a plugin on the Case Close event to post a message to a Service Bus queue (e.g. “case-closed-queue”). An Azure Function with a ServiceBusTrigger picks up each case message. The function reads the case data (here simulated as a simple string message) and can then forward details to a ticketing or tracking system. Below, the function logs the case information from the queue. 

using Microsoft.Azure.WebJobs;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

public static class CaseClosedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("CaseClosedFunction")]
    public static void Run(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("case-closed-queue", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")] string message,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation($"Processing closed case message: {message}");
        // (Code to integrate with a ticketing system could go here)
    }
}

When a Product is updated (Batch Processing)

Concept: On the Product Update event, a CRM workflow could send a message to the “product-updates-queue”. An Azure Function triggers on this queue to handle updates in batch. For example, the function might add the product to a batch job or push it to another system. In the example below, we log the incoming product update message. 

public static class ProductUpdatedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("ProductUpdatedFunction")]
    public static async Task Run(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("product-updates-queue", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")] string message,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation($"Received product update: {message}");
        // (For example, add message to a batch processing list or database)
    }
}

When a Contact is deleted (Archive Data)

Concept: On Contact Delete, CRM can post a summary message to a “contact-deleted-queue”. The Azure Function triggered by this queue could archive the contact’s information (e.g. write to an archival data store). In this sample function, we simply log that the contact data is being archived. 

public static class ContactDeletedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("ContactDeletedFunction")]
    public static void Run(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("contact-deleted-queue", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")] string message,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation($"Archiving deleted contact info: {message}");
        // (Archive logic would go here, such as storing the JSON in long-term storage)
    }
}

4. Using Logic Apps with Azure Functions

Azure Logic Apps is a visual, drag-and-drop workflow platform that can integrate Dynamics 365 (Dataverse) with Azure Functions. You build a Logic App workflow by adding triggers and actions on a canvas (no code needed). Using the Dataverse connector, you can trigger a workflow whenever CRM records change. Then in the workflow you add an HTTP action that calls your Azure Function’s endpoint. This way, CRM events handled by Logic Apps will invoke the Function. Below are some example flows.

For each example, imagine a Logic App workflow that starts with a Dataverse trigger (e.g. "When a record is added/updated") and then uses an HTTP action to call the function.

When an Opportunity is won (Trigger Reward Process)

Concept: Create a Logic App that triggers when an Opportunity record is updated to status “Won”. In the Logic App, add an HTTP action to call an Azure Function with the opportunity details. The function (below) processes the winning opportunity – for example, sending a reward or notification. 

public static class OpportunityWonFunction
{
    [FunctionName("OpportunityWonFunction")]
    public static async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Opportunity won event received.");
        string json = await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync();
        dynamic data = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json);
        string oppName = data?.opportunityname;
        // (Perform reward process here)
        log.LogInformation($"Processed rewards for opportunity: {oppName}");
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

When an Invoice is created (Save PDF to Blob Storage)

Concept: Set up a Logic App trigger on Invoice creation. The Logic App then calls an Azure Function with the invoice data. The function (below) could generate a PDF and save it to Azure Blob Storage. In this example, we simply log that an invoice was created. 

public static class InvoiceCreatedFunction
{
    [FunctionName("InvoiceCreatedFunction")]
    public static async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Invoice created event received.");
        // In a real function, parse req.Body, generate PDF, and upload to Blob Storage
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

When Customer preferences are updated (Sync with Other System)

Concept: Use a Logic App that triggers on update of a Customer Preferences record. The app then calls an Azure Function with the updated preferences. The function code can parse the JSON and push the changes to another system or database. Below, we log that the preferences were updated. 

public static class CustomerPrefsSyncFunction
{
    [FunctionName("CustomerPrefsSyncFunction")]
    public static async Task<IActionResult> Run(
        [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post", Route = null)] HttpRequest req,
        ILogger log)
    {
        log.LogInformation("Customer preferences updated event received.");
        string json = await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync();
        dynamic data = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json);
        // (Sync data with external system)
        log.LogInformation("Customer preferences synchronized.");
        return new OkResult();
    }
}

Each of the above examples shows how an Azure Function (in C#) can tie into Dynamics CRM workflows via webhooks, queues, or Logic Apps. By wiring up triggers on CRM events to Azure Functions, you can extend CRM with custom logic (sending emails, updating other systems, etc.) without managing your own servers. The Concepts above give a high-level flow, and the C# code snippets show how simple the function code can be. This approach keeps the focus on real-world CRM scenarios while avoiding complex setup details.

Sources: Microsoft docs on Azure Functions and Dynamics CRM webhooks/Logic Apps.

azure-2.title: Azure Functions with Dynamics 365: Surviving High-Volume Dataverse Integrations (Part 2)
azure-2.html:
📚 This is Part 2 of my series "Azure Functions with Dynamics 365". New here? Start with Part 1: Beginner tutorial (webhooks, Service Bus, Logic Apps).

Beginner tutorials teach you how to connect two systems. Enterprise architecture teaches you how to keep them from crashing.

When building an enterprise Loan Management System in Dynamics 365, the architecture looks clean on paper: a user creates a loan application, Dataverse fires an asynchronous Webhook, an Azure Function catches the payload, calls a third-party Credit Bureau API, and writes the credit score back to CRM.

In day-to-day operations, handling 5 or 50 loans an hour, this pattern works beautifully.

Then, reality hits: The business decides to bulk import 10,000 historical loan applications.

Unless explicitly filtered or turned off during data migration, Dataverse treats every single imported record as a brand-new "Create" event. In a matter of seconds, Dataverse instantly fires 10,000 concurrent webhooks.

This creates a massive cascade effect across your infrastructure:

  • The Azure Function Flood: Your Function App is instantly slammed with thousands of parallel HTTP execution requests, triggering massive scaling or exhausting available network connections.
  • The Third-Party API Bottleneck: Your function desperately tries to call the external Credit Bureau API 10,000 times at once, instantly triggering rate limits or crashing the vendor's service.
  • The Write-Back Deadlock: Even if the credit checks succeed, your function tries to write 10,000 scores back to Dataverse simultaneously, slamming into Service Protection Limits.

This sudden data surge exposes hidden enterprise traps that will completely take down your integration if you rely on standard out-of-the-box assumptions or naive code.

Developers familiar with data migrations often ask: If we are handling thousands of records, why not just use Azure Data Factory (ADF) or SSIS packages?

The answer comes down to a fundamental architectural rule: Never use a Batch ETL tool for Event-Driven Application Logic.

Why Traditional ETL Tools (SSIS / ADF) Fail for Event-Driven Integrations

  • Batch vs. Real-Time Paradigm Mismatch: ADF/SSIS are built for scheduled, bulk data movement (e.g., migrating a SQL database overnight). They cannot natively listen to real-time Dataverse event triggers the way an HTTP-triggered Azure Function can.
  • Turning ETL into an Anti-Pattern: Forcing ADF to run a For-Each loop calling external Credit Bureau APIs for every single record turns a data pipeline into an unmaintainable, sluggish script.
  • The Error 429 Multiplier: If ADF pushes 10,000 updates back into Dataverse simultaneously without a smart retry mechanism, it will slam into Dataverse Service Protection Limits, flood logs with 429 errors, and corrupt the sync.
  • Lack of Native Webhook Listening: SSIS and ADF cannot act as an open HTTP webhook endpoint out-of-the-box without an intermediary web service catching the payload first.

Architectural Rule of Thumb:

  • Use Azure Data Factory / SSIS for Bulk Data Migration (moving massive tables from Point A to Point B).
  • Use Azure Functions + Webhooks for Application Integration (reacting to CRM events in real-time and calling external APIs).

Why OOB Features Fail Under Heavy Load:

  • Plugins (2-Minute Hard Limit): Execute inside a rigid sandbox. If the external API slows down under 10,000 requests, plugins time out at 120 seconds, crash, and block CRM worker threads, degrading live user performance.
  • Power Automate (Throttling & API Exhaustion): Firing 10,000 concurrent flows rapidly exhausts API entitlements, causing aggressive platform throttling and leaving time-sensitive records stuck in a "Running" state.

Routing this workload to an Azure Function keeps the CRM UI responsive and scales infinitely. However, you must preemptively handle three critical code-level traps:

  1. The "Null Reference" JSON Crash: Dataverse webhooks send a deeply nested RemoteExecutionContext.
  2. Socket Exhaustion: Instantiating a new HttpClient() inside the function for every request will exhaust all available server network sockets.
  3. Dataverse API Throttling (Error 429): Pushing 10,000 scores back simultaneously triggers service protection limits.

A Quick Warning: Dataverse Webhooks will time out after 60 seconds. This setup works great for fast APIs. But if your external credit check API takes longer than 45 seconds to respond, your function will break.

When dealing with slow APIs, you need to decouple the system using Azure Service Bus (which we will cover in Part 3!).

The Production-Ready C# Code

Under the Hood: How Our Code Solves the 3 Enterprise Traps

1. Safe JSON Deserialization (RemoteExecutionContext)

  • The Hidden Risk: When Dataverse fires a webhook, it doesn't send a clean, simple JSON object like {"id": "123"}. It sends a massive, deeply nested payload representing the entire RemoteExecutionContext (containing input parameters, pre-images, post-images, business unit info, user IDs, and context depths). If you try to parse this manually using generic JSON path traversal (like JObject.Parse()["InputParameters"]...), a single missing property or slight schema variation causes an immediate NullReferenceException, crashing the function execution.

  • The Architectural Necessity: Using RemoteExecutionContext from the official Microsoft.Xrm.Sdk provides a strongly-typed contract. Microsoft maintains this object mapping. It guarantees that regardless of the underlying JSON structure changes or complex metadata fields, your function can safely extract core properties like PrimaryEntityId instantly and reliably.

2. Static HttpClient (static readonly)

  • The Hidden Risk: In C#, HttpClient implements IDisposable. A common beginner anti-pattern is instantiating a new client inside the function method (e.g., using (var client = new HttpClient())) or letting it dispose on every request. Under low load, this works fine. But when 10,000 concurrent webhooks hit


  • The Architectural Necessity: Declaring HttpClient as private static readonly forces the Azure Function runtime to reuse a single network connection pool across the entire lifecycle of the worker process. This single architectural change drops network overhead to zero, prevents port exhaustion, and allows your function to handle massive spikes cleanly.

3. Smart 429 Retry-After Handling

  • The Hidden Risk: Microsoft protects Dataverse from being overwhelmed using Service Protection API Limits. If an integration floods Dataverse with 10,000 concurrent update requests (PATCH), the platform instantly blocks the traffic and returns an HTTP 429 Too Many Requests status. If your code treats a 429 like a permanent failure, or worse, blindly retries immediately without pausing, you amplify the traffic spike, extend your lockout period, and leave thousands of loan applications stuck in an unupdated state.

  • The Architectural Necessity: Dataverse doesn't just block you—it tells you how long to wait via the Retry-After HTTP header. By programmatically intercepting the 429, reading that exact header delta, and dynamically pausing execution (await Task.Delay(retryAfter)), your code behaves as a cooperative enterprise citizen. It steps back when the platform is busy, waits out the exact cooldown window, and quietly completes the sync without corrupting data or triggering permanent API blocks.

The Architectural Reality Check: The Self-Inflicted Wound

We’ve engineered the code to survive the chaos:

  • We bypassed null-reference exceptions by safely deserializing through RemoteExecutionContext.
  • We locked down a static readonly HttpClient to prevent server socket exhaustion.
  • We built smart retry loops that intercept HTTP 429s and respect the platform's Retry-After header.

Your Azure Function is now a masterclass in enterprise resilience.

And yet... the system still strains if you miss the ultimate rule:

Why were your real-time webhooks even active during a 10,000-record historical data import in the first place?

The best code isn't the most clever code—it's the code you never have to force into the wrong pattern.

If you are running a massive historical migration, letting Dataverse fire 10,000 real-time webhooks for data that is already years old is an architectural self-inflicted wound. No amount of C# optimization will save you if you use real-time, event-driven patterns for batch-level events.

Rule #1 of Enterprise Architecture: Disable your webhook steps during data migrations, stage your data cleanly, and reserve real-time webhooks strictly for live, transactional user events.

What Happens When the Vendor Goes Dark?

Even with your webhooks safely restricted to live transactions, a new enterprise nightmare looms.

What happens when your external Credit Bureau API goes down for a 2-hour maintenance window while live loan applications are flooding in? A direct synchronous webhook will time out, fail, and drop the data unless something is holding the message safely in transit.

That requires decoupling the producer from the consumer entirely.

...And that brings us to the edge of Part 3.

azure-3.html:
📚 This is Part 3 of my series "Azure Functions with Dynamics 365". New here? Start with Part 1, or read the previous one: Part 2: Surviving high-volume integrations.

Processing enterprise-scale batch workloads against Microsoft Dataverse exposes the architectural boundary between transactional business applications and distributed computing engines. When an enterprise platform must process hundreds of thousands of operational records within a fixed maintenance window, standard extension models fail.

This guide provides an end-to-end architectural blueprint for engineering high-scale, stateful, and fault-tolerant batch systems using Azure Durable Functions and the Durable Task Framework (DTFx) to orchestrate complex Dataverse transactions.

Consider a Tier-1 financial services system managing active consumer and commercial loan portfolios implemented on Microsoft Dataverse. Every day at 00:00 UTC, the core ledger engine processes the active loan portfolio:

  • Active Records: 250,000 active loan agreements.
  • Per-Record Operations:
  • Retrieve active contract parameters (current principal balance, indexed interest rates, penalty rules, grace periods).
  • Compute daily accrued interest using fractional day-count conventions
  • Evaluate delinquent repayment schedules and calculate compound late penalties.
  • Create an immutable double-entry financial ledger transaction in Dataverse (fin_ledgerentry).
  • Update the parent loan account (fin_loanaccount) with accrued totals, roll-up balances, and timestamp metadata.

  • Service Level Agreement (SLA):
  • Total batch execution must terminate within a strict 4-hour maintenance window (00:00 UTC to 04:00 UTC) prior to regional banking integrations.
  • Core Non-Negotiable Constraint: Exactly-Once Processing. Under no condition may a network failure, machine restart, or runtime timeout cause an account to accrue double interest or generate duplicated ledger postings.
  • The Architecture of Failure: Why Standard CRM Patterns Collapse Under High-Volume Loads
  • Before designing a highly scalable system, a Solution Architect must first deeply understand exactly how and why systems break. When processing massive datasets—such as recalculating 250,000 active loan records at midnight—relying on standard Microsoft Power Platform or Dynamics 365 extensibility points will result in catastrophic system failure.
  • Below is an engineering evaluation of why familiar primitives collapse at this scale.

1. The Synchronous Plugin: The 120-Second Sandbox Kill-Switch

Many developers attempt to trigger a synchronous plugin on a batch update or a custom action.

How it fails: Dynamics 365 plugins execute within an isolated, resource-constrained sandbox worker process (Microsoft.Crm.Sandbox.WorkerProcess.exe). Microsoft enforces a non-negotiable 120-second timeout limit to protect the shared multi-tenant SQL Server cluster from runaway queries.

The Infrastructure Reality: If your loop processes record number 4,200 and hits the 120-second mark, the Sandbox Host aggressively terminates the thread.

The Collateral Damage: Because synchronous plugins run within the main database transaction, the SQL Server must roll back the entire execution. Rolling back 4,200 complex records causes massive database locking, blocking other users and external integrations from reading or writing to those tables while the rollback completes.

2. The Asynchronous Plugin: The AsyncOperationBase Black Hole

Realizing synchronous plugins time out, developers often offload the workload to Asynchronous Plugins or classic Background Workflows, firing off 250,000 individual async jobs.

  • How it fails: Every async job generated in Dataverse is written to the physical SQL database in the AsyncOperationBase table.
  • The Infrastructure Reality: Dropping 250,000 jobs instantly into this table causes sudden, massive database bloat. The Dataverse Asynchronous Processing Service (which operates on a FIFO/priority queue) is suddenly overwhelmed.
  • The Collateral Damage (Queue Starvation): The Async Service doesn't just run your custom code; it is the heartbeat of the CRM. It processes SLAs, email sending, cascade deletes, and system jobs. By flooding the queue with a batch calculation, you cause Queue Starvation. Emails stop sending, SLAs miss their targets, and the entire CRM system degrades to a crawl for business users while the queue churns for the next 14 hours.

3. Power Automate (Cloud Flows): API Exhaustion and 429 Throttling

Power Automate is exceptional for business logic, but it is not an ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) or heavy-compute engine. Using an "Apply to each" loop for 250,000 records introduces severe API limitations.

  • How it fails: Power Automate execution is strictly metered. Every action inside a loop counts against the tenant's Power Platform Request limits. If you have 4 actions inside a loop running 250,000 times, you immediately consume 1,000,000 API calls.
  • The Infrastructure Reality: You will violently hit the Service Protection API Limits. Dataverse allows a maximum of 6,000 requests per 5-minute window per user. Once breached, Dataverse responds with an HTTP 429 Too Many Requests error.
  • The Collateral Damage: The flow halts, goes into a forced suspension (Retry-After backoff), and what should be a 3-hour job stretches into a multi-day execution. Furthermore, massive loops in Power Automate consume immense workflow memory, often causing the flow execution to time out or crash silently after 30 days.

4. Stateless Azure Functions: The "Partial Commit" Nightmare

To avoid CRM limits entirely, the logical next step is writing a custom Azure Function (on a standard Consumption plan) to pull the records and process them externally.

  • How it fails: Standard Azure Functions are stateless. They have a hard maximum execution time of 5 to 10 minutes. If you process records sequentially, the Azure fabric will forcefully terminate the host container at the timeout mark.
  • The Infrastructure Reality: Even if you upgrade to a Premium plan with unlimited execution time, you are at the mercy of the cloud. The underlying virtual machine might need a security patch, or the Azure Load Balancer might drop the connection after 230 seconds of idle network time. The server reboots, and the function dies instantly.
  • The Collateral Damage: Because the function is stateless, it has total amnesia. If it crashes after processing 134,000 out of 250,000 accounts, how do you resume the job safely? If you just restart the function, you will double-charge interest on the first 134,000 accounts, corrupting your financial ledger. To prevent this, you would have to engineer incredibly complex, custom tracking tables and checkpoint logic within Dataverse itself—essentially reinventing the wheel.

3. High-Throughput Serverless Architecture: The Fan-Out / Fan-In Topology

  • To achieve high throughput, strict determinism, and complete resilience against compute drops, the workload is decoupled into a Durable Functions Fan-Out / Fan-In pattern.

Component Roles Across the Lifecycle

The Timer Client: Triggers at 00:00 UTC and invokes IDurableOrchestrationClient.StartNewAsync(), passing batch run parameters.

The Orchestrator: Calls a metadata activity to query Dataverse and fetch the primary keys of all 250,000 eligible accounts.

  1. Splits the 250,000 IDs into 500 discrete chunks containing 500 records each.
  2. Dispatches 500 parallel activity tasks via Task.WhenAll().

The Activity Functions (Workers):Each activity receives an isolated slice of 500 record IDs.

  1. Executes business math in-memory.
  2. Packages database updates into transactional payloads using the Dataverse SDK (ExecuteTransactionRequest or ExecuteMultipleRequest).
  3. Returns a structured processing summary to the orchestrator.
  4. The Aggregator (Fan-In): The orchestrator resumes upon completion of all 500 activity tasks, aggregates execution metrics (total successes, throughput per minute, failed account arrays), and writes a consolidated run log into Dataverse.

Under the Hood: The Durable Task Framework (DTFx) & Event Sourcing

Durable Functions does not keep compute threads active in memory while waiting for sub-tasks to finish. Understanding this mechanism requires looking under the hood at the Durable Task Framework (DTFx).

The Task Hub

  • The orchestration state is isolated within a logical boundary called a Task Hub. In standard deployments, the Task Hub consists of storage resources managed by the runtime:
  • Control Queues: Ordered queues used to deliver lifecycle messages to orchestrators.
  • Work-Item Queues: Queues dedicated to dispatching tasks to Activity Functions. When an orchestrator calls an activity, it drops an execution payload onto a work-item queue.
  • History Table: An Azure Table Storage instance storing the event-sourced log of every state transition that occurs inside the orchestration.

The Event Sourcing & Replay Engine

Durable Functions implements the Event Sourcing Pattern. State is not persisted as a mutated object; rather, every lifecycle action is appended to an append-only log.

The Step-by-Step Replay Lifecycle

  1. Invocation: The orchestrator starts running code from line 1.
  2. Reaching an Await: The orchestrator encounters an await for an Activity.
  3. Yield and Dehydration: The framework checks its execution history. On first run, the activity has not completed. A record is written to the History table (TaskScheduled), and the orchestrator runtime flushes its state, terminates the execution thread, and yields compute resources. You pay nothing while the activity executes.
  4. Activity Completion: The worker finishes and writes its result payload to storage. It puts an orchestration wake-up message onto the Control Queue.
  5. The Replay (Hydration):

  • The orchestrator wakes up.
  • It starts executing again from Line 1 of the function code.
  • When it reaches the line calling the Activity, it consults the local history log.
  • The log indicates that the Activity has already executed and contains the cached result list.
  • The orchestrator skips re-executing the activity, instantly assigns the cached output to the variable, and proceeds to the next line of code.

5. The Golden Constraint: Determinism in Orchestrators

Because the Orchestrator function reconstructs its state by re-running its code from the beginning during every single replay, the code path must be 100% deterministic. If re-executing the code on a different server at a different millisecond takes a different branch, the event-sourcing graph desynchronizes.

  • System Time: DateTime.UtcNow evaluates differently on every replay. context.CurrentUtcDateTime returns the timestamp recorded during the initial scheduling of that step.
  • Random Identifiers: Guid.NewGuid() generates a different ID during a replay, causing foreign key mismatches. context.NewGuid() generates a deterministic GUID based on the orchestration instance ID and execution step count.
  • Direct I/O: Network calls can fail or return different data on a replay. All Dataverse ServiceClient calls must be strictly isolated inside the Activity Functions.

6. Enterprise Integration with Dataverse: Concurrency, Throttling & SDK Optimizations

  • Fanning out hundreds of concurrent Activity Functions against a Microsoft Dataverse tenant requires fine-grained control to prevent crushing the Dataverse Web API.

1. Dataverse Service Protection Limits & HTTP 429:To protect shared multi-tenant infrastructure, Dataverse enforces Service Protection Limits (e.g., maximum 6,000 requests per 5-minute window, max 52 concurrent execution requests per web-server tier). Exceeding these triggers an HTTP status code 429 (Too Many Requests).

2. : To prevent the Fan-Out pattern from overwhelming Dataverse, global concurrency must be constrained inside the function app's configuration:

By locking maxConcurrentActivityFunctionEvaluations to 32, even if the orchestrator dispatches 500 tasks simultaneously, the runtime host will only lease and execute 32 activity work-items at any single instant.

3. Connection Pooling and SNAT Port Exhaustion

Creating a new ServiceClient instance inside every activity invocation will rapidly exhaust the underlying Azure App Service worker's outbound SNAT ports.

  • Architecture Requirement: The Dataverse ServiceClient must be registered as a Singleton using standard Azure Functions Dependency Injection. This manages connection pooling across all concurrent Activity Function runs, eliminating socket leaks.

7. Production-Grade Implementation (C#)

Below is a complete, enterprise-grade implementation demonstrating deterministic orchestration, activity batching, native backoff retries, and transactional Dataverse operations using the isolated worker model.

1. The Orchestrator Implementation 

C#
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker;
using Microsoft.DurableTask;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

namespace FinTech.Lms.Orchestrations
{
    public static class LoanProcessingOrchestrator
    {
        [Function(nameof(RunLoanPortfolioOrchestrator))]
        public static async Task<BatchExecutionSummary> RunLoanPortfolioOrchestrator(
            [OrchestrationTrigger] TaskOrchestrationContext context)
        {
            ILogger logger = context.CreateReplaySafeLogger(nameof(LoanProcessingOrchestrator));
            logger.LogInformation("Orchestration started. Execution ID: {instanceId}", context.InstanceId);

            // Step 1: Query eligible loan IDs (Deterministic: All I/O offloaded to activity)
            var eligibleLoanIds = await context.CallActivityAsync<List<Guid>>(
                nameof(QueryEligibleLoanIdsActivity), 
                null);

            if (eligibleLoanIds == null || !eligibleLoanIds.Any())
            {
                logger.LogWarning("No eligible loan records found. Terminating orchestration.");
                return new BatchExecutionSummary { TotalProcessed = 0, SuccessCount = 0, FailureCount = 0 };
            }

            // Step 2: Partition dataset into balanced chunks of 500 records
            const int chunkSize = 500;
            var chunks = eligibleLoanIds
                .Select((id, index) => new { id, index })
                .GroupBy(x => x.index / chunkSize)
                .Select(g => g.Select(x => x.id).ToList())
                .ToList();

            // Configure resilient retry options for activities encountering Dataverse throttling
            var activityRetryOptions = TaskOptions.FromRetryPolicy(new TaskRetryPolicy(
                maxNumberOfAttempts: 5,
                firstRetryInterval: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5),
                backoffCoefficient: 2.0,
                maxRetryInterval: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)));

            // Step 3: FAN-OUT. Dispatch parallel Activity tasks across workers
            var processingTasks = new List<Task<ChunkResult>>();
            for (int i = 0; i < chunks.Count; i++)
            {
                var payload = new ChunkProcessingRequest
                {
                    ChunkIndex = i + 1,
                    TotalChunks = chunks.Count,
                    LoanIds = chunks[i],
                    // Generate deterministic timestamp through context, NEVER DateTime.UtcNow
                    CalculationTimestamp = context.CurrentUtcDateTime
                };

                processingTasks.Add(context.CallActivityAsync<ChunkResult>(
                    nameof(ProcessLoanChunkActivity), 
                    payload, 
                    activityRetryOptions));
            }

            // Step 4: FAN-IN. Await completion of all concurrent activities
            ChunkResult[] results = await Task.WhenAll(processingTasks);

            // Step 5: Aggregate results
            var finalSummary = new BatchExecutionSummary
            {
                TotalProcessed = results.Sum(r => r.RecordsProcessed),
                SuccessCount = results.Sum(r => r.SuccessCount),
                FailureCount = results.Sum(r => r.FailedCount),
                FailedRecordIds = results.SelectMany(r => r.FailedIds).ToList(),
                CompletedAt = context.CurrentUtcDateTime
            };

            // Step 6: Persist audit log back into Dataverse via dedicated final activity
            await context.CallActivityAsync(nameof(PersistBatchRunSummaryActivity), finalSummary);

            return finalSummary;
        }
    }

    public class ChunkProcessingRequest
    {
        public int ChunkIndex { get; set; }
        public int TotalChunks { get; set; }
        public List<Guid> LoanIds { get; set; }
        public DateTime CalculationTimestamp { get; set; }
    }

    public class ChunkResult
    {
        public int RecordsProcessed { get; set; }
        public int SuccessCount { get; set; }
        public int FailedCount { get; set; }
        public List<Guid> FailedIds { get; set; } = new();
    }

    public class BatchExecutionSummary
    {
        public int TotalProcessed { get; set; }
        public int SuccessCount { get; set; }
        public int FailureCount { get; set; }
        public List<Guid> FailedRecordIds { get; set; } = new();
        public DateTime CompletedAt { get; set; }
    }
}


2. The Activity Worker Implementation 

C#
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using Microsoft.PowerPlatform.Dataverse.Client;
using Microsoft.Xrm.Sdk;
using Microsoft.Xrm.Sdk.Messages;

namespace FinTech.Lms.Orchestrations
{
    public class LoanActivities
    {
        private readonly ServiceClient _dataverseClient;
        private readonly ILogger<LoanActivities> _logger;

        // ServiceClient injected as Singleton via Dependency Injection
        public LoanActivities(ServiceClient dataverseClient, ILogger<LoanActivities> logger)
        {
            _dataverseClient = dataverseClient ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(dataverseClient));
            _logger = logger;
        }

        [Function(nameof(ProcessLoanChunkActivity))]
        public async Task<ChunkResult> ProcessLoanChunkActivity(
            [ActivityTrigger] ChunkProcessingRequest request)
        {
            var result = new ChunkResult();

            // Create batch execution request to minimize network roundtrips to Dataverse
            var multipleRequest = new ExecuteMultipleRequest
            {
                Requests = new OrganizationRequestCollection(),
                Settings = new ExecuteMultipleSettings
                {
                    ContinueOnError = true,
                    ReturnResponses = true
                }
            };

            foreach (var loanId in request.LoanIds)
            {
                // In-memory calculations (interest, late fees, balances)
                decimal dailyInterest = CalculateAccruedInterest(loanId);

                // 1. Prepare Ledger Entry Entity
                var ledgerEntry = new Entity("fin_ledgerentry")
                {
                    Attributes =
                    {
                        ["fin_loanaccountid"] = new EntityReference("fin_loanaccount", loanId),
                        ["fin_amount"] = new Money(dailyInterest),
                        ["fin_entrytype"] = new OptionSetValue(100000001), 
                        ["fin_transactiondate"] = request.CalculationTimestamp
                    }
                };

                // 2. Prepare Parent Account Update
                var accountUpdate = new Entity("fin_loanaccount", loanId)
                {
                    Attributes =
                    {
                        ["fin_lastinterestaccrualdate"] = request.CalculationTimestamp,
                        ["fin_accruedinterestbalance"] = new Money(dailyInterest) 
                    }
                };

                multipleRequest.Requests.Add(new CreateRequest { Target = ledgerEntry });
                multipleRequest.Requests.Add(new UpdateRequest { Target = accountUpdate });
            }

            // Execute batch against Dataverse Web API
            var response = (ExecuteMultipleResponse)await _dataverseClient.ExecuteAsync(multipleRequest);

            // Parse responses to collect individual operational failures
            foreach (var responseItem in response.Responses)
            {
                if (responseItem.Fault != null)
                {
                    result.FailedCount++;
                    _logger.LogError("Dataverse batch item fault: {message}", responseItem.Fault.Message);
                }
                else
                {
                    result.SuccessCount++;
                }
            }

            result.RecordsProcessed = request.LoanIds.Count;
            return result;
        }

        private decimal CalculateAccruedInterest(Guid loanId)
        {
            return 12.50m;
        }
    }
}

azure-5.title: Azure Functions with Dynamics 365: Retries, Dead-Letter Queues and Duplicate Handling (Part 5)
azure-5.html:
📚 This is Part 5 of my series "Azure Functions with Dynamics 365". New here? Start with Part 1, or read the previous one: Part 4: Webhooks vs Service Bus for Dataverse events.

Why this part comes next

In Part 4, Dataverse pushed every new loan application out to Azure, and our Function fetched the credit score from the bureau and wrote it back. The demo worked perfectly. Production is where things fail.

The scenario

It's month-end. The bank imports 3,000 loan applications from a partner portal in 20 minutes. Halfway through, the credit bureau's API starts returning 503 Service Unavailable for 8 minutes. Then three things happen:

  • About 1,100 events fail. If nothing retries them, 1,100 loans sit with an empty credit score, and loan officers start calling the IT team.
  • Twelve records have bad data, for example a PAN in the wrong format. The bureau rejects them every single time. If they keep retrying, they block nothing but waste calls and fill the logs.
  • Some events arrive twice. A Function times out after writing the score but before confirming the message, so Service Bus delivers it again. Without protection, the bureau is called twice and the bank pays twice.

Part 4 ended with "make the Function safe to run twice". This part shows how, step by step, with the same loan scenario and C# code. The rule we're working towards: retry what might succeed, park what never will, and never do the same work twice.

Three kinds of failure

Every failure in an integration falls into one of three groups. The fix is different for each, so the first job of your code is to tell them apart.

  • Transient. Example: the bureau returns 503 or 429, a network timeout, Dataverse throttling (429). Will a retry help? Yes, later. What to do: retry with a delay.
  • Permanent (poison). Example: invalid PAN, loan record deleted, a required field is empty. Will a retry help? No, never. What to do: stop retrying, park it with a reason, alert a person.
  • Duplicate. Example: the same event delivered twice after a timeout or retry. Will a retry help? It already did. What to do: detect it and skip the work.

Simple picture: a courier delivering parcels. If nobody is home, he tries again tomorrow (transient). If the address doesn't exist, he returns the parcel to the depot with a note (poison, dead-letter). If the parcel was already delivered, he doesn't deliver it again (duplicate).

What happens to a failed event


On the Service Bus path, every event ends in one of three places: scored once, retried after the lock expires, or parked in the dead-letter queue where a person sees it. The webhook path is different, and we'll come back to it after the hands-on.

Hands-on 1: Set up the queue for retries and dead-lettering

What you need: the Service Bus namespace, queue and Dataverse service endpoint from Part 4 (Hands-on 2), and the Function project from Part 4.

With a Service Bus queue, retries come built in. The Function receives the message in peek-lock mode: Service Bus hides it for a while (the lock) and waits. If the Function completes it, it's removed. If the Function fails or the lock runs out, the message becomes visible again and is delivered again. Each attempt increases its delivery count. When the count reaches the max delivery count, Service Bus moves the message to the queue's dead-letter queue automatically.

Step 1: Set the queue properties

Azure portal → Service Bus namespace → Queues → loan-events → Properties:

  • Max delivery count: 5. Enough to ride out a short outage, small enough that poison messages don't loop for long.
  • Message lock duration: 3 minutes. Longer than the slowest bureau call plus the Dataverse update.
  • Dead-lettering on message expiration: On. Messages that expire are kept, not silently deleted.
  • Message time to live: 1 day. An unprocessed loan event older than a day needs a person, not a retry.

Step 2: Know where the dead letters go

Every queue has a built-in sub-queue at loan-events/$DeadLetterQueue. You don't create it. In the portal, open the queue and select Service Bus Explorer → Dead-letter to peek at messages, their delivery count and the reason they were parked.

Step 3: Don't add a second retry layer

Azure Functions retry policies ([FixedDelayRetry], [ExponentialBackoffRetry]) are supported only for a few triggers, such as Timer, Event Hubs, Kafka and Cosmos DB. For a Service Bus trigger, the queue's delivery count is the retry mechanism. Stacking your own retry loop on top of it multiplies the attempts (5 deliveries × 5 inner retries = 25 bureau calls for one loan).

Hands-on 2: A Function that knows the difference

In Part 4, LoanEventProcessor left two TODOs and relied on one rule: if the method throws, Service Bus delivers the message again. That treats a bureau outage and an invalid PAN the same way. Now we fill in those TODOs and settle each message ourselves, so we decide what happens to it.

Step 1: Turn off auto-complete

By default, the Service Bus trigger completes the message when the Function succeeds and abandons it when it throws. We switch that off with AutoCompleteMessages = false and use ServiceBusMessageActions to complete, dead-letter or leave each message. (Isolated worker model, as in Part 4. Settling messages yourself needs version 5.14 or later of the Service Bus extension.)

Step 2: Sort the errors 

using Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus;
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

public class LoanEventProcessor(
    ICreditBureauClient bureau,
    ILoanRepository loans,
    ILogger<LoanEventProcessor> log)
{
    [Function("LoanEventProcessor")]
    public async Task Run(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("loan-events", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection",
            AutoCompleteMessages = false)] ServiceBusReceivedMessage message,
        ServiceBusMessageActions actions)
    {
        var context = DataverseContextParser.Parse(message.Body); // helper from Part 2
        var loanId = context.PrimaryEntityId;

        try
        {
            var loan = await loans.GetAsync(loanId)
                ?? throw new PermanentFailureException($"Loan {loanId} no longer exists");

            if (!PanValidator.IsValid(loan.Pan))
                throw new PermanentFailureException($"Invalid PAN on loan {loan.Number}");

            // Hands-on 3 adds the duplicate check here

            var score = await bureau.GetScoreAsync(loan.Pan); // 503, 429, timeout = transient
            await loans.SaveScoreAsync(loanId, score, context.OperationId);

            await actions.CompleteMessageAsync(message);
        }
        catch (PermanentFailureException ex)
        {
            log.LogError(ex, "Poison loan event {LoanId}", loanId);
            await actions.DeadLetterMessageAsync(message,
                deadLetterReason: "PermanentFailure",
                deadLetterErrorDescription: ex.Message);
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (IsTransient(ex))
        {
            // Don't complete, don't abandon: the lock expires after 3 minutes
            // and Service Bus delivers the message again.
            log.LogWarning(ex, "Transient failure for {LoanId}, delivery {Count} of 5",
                loanId, message.DeliveryCount);
        }
    }

    private static bool IsTransient(Exception ex) =>
        ex is TransientFailureException or HttpRequestException or TaskCanceledException;
}

Step 3: Why we don't abandon transient failures

AbandonMessageAsync makes the message available immediately. During an 8-minute bureau outage, five immediate retries are used up in a few seconds and every loan ends up dead-lettered. By leaving the message alone, the 3-minute lock becomes a built-in delay: five deliveries spread over about twelve minutes, which covers the 8-minute outage in our scenario. For longer outages, send a copy with a later ScheduledEnqueueTime and complete the original, so you control the backoff yourself.

What about Dataverse throttling?

When the Function writes the score back, Dataverse may answer 429 Too Many Requests during a big import. The ServiceClient retries 429s for you using the Retry-After value, as we saw in Part 2. If it still fails after its own retries, it counts as transient here.

Hands-on 3: Make the Function safe to run twice

Both webhooks and Service Bus are at least once: an event can arrive more than once. The classic case: the Function saves the score, then the lock expires before CompleteMessageAsync runs, and the same message comes back. The answer is idempotency: running the same event twice has the same result as running it once.

Step 1: Pick a key that identifies the event

The Dataverse execution context carries an OperationId for the system job that sent the event. When Dataverse retries the same job, the OperationId stays the same. That makes it a good idempotency key for one loan event.

Step 2: Store it with the result

Add a text column to the Loan Application table, new_scoreoperationid. When the Function saves the score, it saves the OperationId in the same update. One update means the score and the key are written together or not at all.

Step 3: Check before doing the work 

// Inside the try block, before calling the bureau
if (loan.ScoreOperationId == context.OperationId)
{
    log.LogInformation("Duplicate event for {LoanId}, already scored", loanId);
    await actions.CompleteMessageAsync(message); // remove it, don't re-do it
    return;
}

Now a duplicate costs one Dataverse read instead of a paid bureau call and a second update.

Other ways to get the same safety

  • Natural check: for this loan scenario, "the loan already has a score from today" is often enough, as mentioned in Part 4.
  • Upsert with an alternate key: when the Function creates records (for example, a Credit Check row per loan), an upsert on an alternate key such as the loan number can't create a second row.
  • A processed-events store: for integrations that touch several systems, keep the processed keys in a small table (Azure Table Storage or a Dataverse table) and check it first.

What doesn't work: checking in memory. A Function app can run on several instances at once, and each one has its own memory.

Hands-on 4: Don't let dead letters die quietly

A dead-letter queue nobody watches is just a slower way to lose data. Our 12 invalid PANs need a person, and the people who can fix them are loan officers, not Azure admins.

Step 1: A Function on the dead-letter queue 

[Function("LoanEventsDeadLetter")]
public async Task HandleDeadLetter(
    [ServiceBusTrigger("loan-events/$DeadLetterQueue", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")]
    ServiceBusReceivedMessage message)
{
    var context = DataverseContextParser.Parse(message.Body);

    // errors: an IIntegrationErrorRepository, injected like loans in Hands-on 2.
    // Create an Integration Error row in Dataverse that loan officers can see in a view
    await errors.CreateAsync(new IntegrationError
    {
        LoanId = context.PrimaryEntityId,
        Reason = message.DeadLetterReason,
        Details = message.DeadLetterErrorDescription,
        Attempts = message.DeliveryCount,
        OperationId = context.OperationId
    });
}

The loan officer sees "Invalid PAN on loan LN-20481" in a Dataverse view, fixes the PAN on the form, and that update fires a new event that goes through the normal path. No one has to open the Azure portal.

Step 2: Alert when the dead-letter count rises

In the Service Bus namespace → Alerts → Create alert rule, use the metric Count of dead-lettered messages in a Queue/Topic, filtered to loan-events, and alert when it's greater than 0. Send it to the support team's email or Teams channel.

Step 3: Replay after a long outage

If the bureau was down for hours, healthy loans may have been dead-lettered as transient failures. Once it's back, resubmit those messages to the main queue (Service Bus Explorer can re-send messages, or use a small replay script). Hands-on 3 makes this safe: any loan that was already scored is skipped.

The webhook path: your status code is the message

With a webhook (Part 4, Hands-on 1) there is no queue and no dead-letter queue. Dataverse calls the Function directly, so the HTTP status code the Function returns is the only thing Dataverse understands.

  • Function returns 200 / 204. Async webhook step: the system job succeeds. Sync webhook step: the save continues.
  • Function returns 5xx or times out. Async step: Dataverse retries the system job, then marks it Failed in System Jobs. Sync step: the save fails and is rolled back; the user sees an error.
  • Function returns 4xx. Async step: treated as a failure as well. Sync step: the save fails and is rolled back.

So, on a webhook:

  • Transient: return 503 and let the async system job be retried.
  • Poison: don't return an error that makes it retry forever. Return 200, and write an Integration Error row (as in Hands-on 4), so a person sees it.
  • Duplicate: the same OperationId check from Hands-on 3 works here too.

Where do failed webhook calls end up? In Settings → System Jobs, filtered to failed jobs. That's a much weaker dead-letter queue: no alert by default, no easy replay, and admins have to look for it. This is one more reason why Part 4 recommended Service Bus when the receiver might be down or the volume is high.

Verify in your environment: check the OperationId in the trace logs of a retried system job before relying on it as your key. If yours changes between retries, use the loan ID plus the record's modifiedon value instead.

Webhook vs Service Bus when things fail

  • Who retries. Webhook: the Dataverse async service (async steps only). Service Bus: Service Bus, up to your max delivery count.
  • Control over delay. Webhook: none. Service Bus: lock duration, or scheduled re-send.
  • Where failures end up. Webhook: failed system jobs in Dataverse. Service Bus: the dead-letter queue, with reason and delivery count.
  • Alerting. Webhook: build it yourself. Service Bus: built-in metric for dead-lettered messages.
  • Replay after an outage. Webhook: hard. Service Bus: re-send from the dead-letter queue.
  • Duplicates. Possible on both.

Rule of thumb: retry what might succeed, park what never will, and never do the same work twice. If a lost or doubled event costs money, put Service Bus in between and make the Function idempotent.

Common mistakes

  1. Treating every error the same. An invalid PAN retried five times is five wasted bureau calls and a delay before anyone sees it.
  2. Abandoning transient failures. The message comes back immediately, and the retries are gone before the outage ends.
  3. A retry loop inside the Function on top of Service Bus retries. Attempts multiply, and the lock can expire mid-loop, which creates duplicates.
  4. Lock duration shorter than the work. The message is delivered again while the first attempt is still running.
  5. No idempotency. Every retry or redelivery calls the bureau again and may write twice.
  6. Nobody watching the dead-letter queue. Messages expire or sit there for weeks. Alert on a count greater than 0.
  7. Returning 500 for poison data on a webhook. Dataverse keeps retrying something that can never succeed.
  8. Dead-letter details only in Azure. The people who can fix the data are business users. Show them the error in Dataverse.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a transient and a poison message, and how does your code treat each? (Hint: retry vs dead-letter with a reason.)
  2. What happens to a Service Bus message when the Function throws, and when does it go to the dead-letter queue? (Hint: peek-lock, delivery count, max delivery count.)
  3. Why can abandoning a message make an outage worse? (Hint: immediate redelivery uses up the retries in seconds.)
  4. Service Bus is "at least once". How do you stop a loan being scored twice? (Hint: an idempotency key saved with the result, checked before the work.)
  5. A webhook-triggered Function gets invalid data. What status code should it return, and why? (Hint: not one that makes Dataverse retry forever.)
  6. The bureau was down for three hours and 900 messages were dead-lettered. How do you recover? (Hint: fix the cause, replay from the dead-letter queue, and rely on idempotency to skip the ones already done.)

Conclusion

In the month-end import, nothing was lost. The 1,100 loans hit by the outage were retried over about twelve minutes and scored once the bureau came back. The 12 invalid PANs were parked with a reason and shown to loan officers in Dataverse. The duplicates were skipped with one read each, and the bank paid for each credit check once.

None of that needed new technology. It needed three decisions in the code: is this failure worth retrying, where does it go if not, and have I already done this work?

Over to you: what's the worst failure you've seen in a live Dataverse integration, and how did you find out about it? Tell me in the comments. 👇
